Enzymatic Kinetic Resolution (EKR) of α-Allenols
(S)( R)
Received: 14.09.2023
Accepted after revision: 30.10.2023
Published online: 27.11.2023 (Version of Record)
DOI: 10.1055/s-0042-1751525; Art ID: ST-2023-09-0402-L
Abstract Enzymatic kinetic resolution (EKR) of racemates has been
considered as an effici ent and scalable technolo gy to deliver enantio-
pure substances in an environmentally benign way. Herein, we develop
a practical EKR of -allenols enabled by a commercially available immo-
bilized lipase, Lipozyme TL-IM. The stereoselectivity factor ( S-factor) of
this kinetic resolution (KR) was investigated to reach up to >1000. The
robust nature of the EKR strategy is reflected by a broad scope of -alle-
nol substrates with the excellent control of enantioselectivity. This
method offers an alternative approach to access chiral -allenols, which
can be easily transformed into many valuable oxycycles.
Keywords enzymatic kinetic resolution (EKR), -allenols, lipase, kinet-
ic resolution, enzymes
Enzymatic kinetic resolution (EKR) is one of the most
practical and industrially wide spread tools in the separa-
tion of enantiomers.1,2 In particular, lipase-catalyzed kinet-
i c  r e s o l u t i o n  ( K R )  h a s  b e e n  d e m o n s t r a t e d  a s  a n  e f f i c i e n t
and scalable approach to produce chiral secondary alcohols,
and its use of less toxic solvents and enzymes presents as
an environmentally benign and atom economical approach
to produce optically active compounds.
3 On the other hand,
chiral -allenols have been widely used as building blocks
in synthetic chemistry, and it can also be easily converted
into diverse and valuable chiral oxycycles (Scheme 1a). 4,5
Previous methods to chiral -allenols were mainly focused
on the allenation of terminal alkynes (ATA) 6,7 starting from
chiral propargylic alcohols, which could be conveniently
obtained from racemic propargylic alcohols via EKR (path a,
Scheme 1b).
8 Direct resolution of racemic -allenols pres-
ents as an alternative and practical method with the forma-
tion of enantiopure compounds at a late stage, which can
improve the tolerance of functional groups, and avoid the
possible loss of enantiopurity du ring the late-stage allena-
tion step, generally requiring relatively harsh conditions. 7
However, very limited approaches were realized for the di-
rect EKR of -allenols, given the fact that the bulky allene
unit does not fit well as the medium-sized group into the
active site of typical lipases,  thus leading to low enantiose-
lectivity.
9,10 In 2015, the Bäckvall group described an enan-
tioselective access to 2,3-dihydrofurans from -allenols by
cascade catalysis, where homemade IL1-PS realized the EKR
of racemic -allenols in the first step. 11 It is noteworthy to
mention that the use of commercially available catalyst en-
dows the developed methods with convenience and higher
possibilities for potential appl ications in other laboratories
and industry as well. Furthermore, immobilization of the li-
pase catalyst would highly improve its practical application
value in industry, due to the recyclability and reusability. In
2016, Hong, Huang, and co-workers elegantly reported
commercially available lipase AK-catalyzed direct and effi-
cient EKR of -allenols, while, relatively low enantioselec-
tivity was observed for electron-rich substrates.
12 Herein,
we report our recent obse rvations on the EKR of -allenols
enabled by a commercially available immobilized lipase, Li-
pozyme TL-IM, exhibiting high  efficiency and selectivity in
the resolution of -allenols.
Preparation of Racemic -Allenols rac-1a–m via ATA 
Reactions
Our work began with the synthesis of racemic -alle-
nols rac-1 via one-step ATA reactions.7b Under the standard
conditions, rac-1a–m could be conveniently obtained from
propargylic alcohols rac-2a–m in 37–91% yields (Scheme
2).

Optimization of the EKR Reaction Conditions
Next, a collection of biocatalysts was studied for the EKR
of -allenol 1a with vinyl acetate as acyl donor in toluene at
35 °C for 14 h, and S-factor was calculated to evaluate lipase
performance in the catalytic esterification (Table 1). The re-
action with Lipozyme TL-IM gave the highest S-factor (637),
which is almost three times as high as S-factor (242) from
the reaction catalyzed by lipase AK. Lipozyme TL-IM, origi-
nating from Thermomyces lanuginosus , is a commercially
available and low-cost lipase, which is immobilized on a
noncompressible silica gel carrier. To our delight, reaction
with lower lipase loading gave even higher enantioselectiv-
ity, and cyclohexane was suggested to be the best solvent to
deliver >99% ee for both ester product (R)-3a and recovered
(S)-1a, exhibiting >1000 of S-factor at this stage. By pro-
longing the reaction time, lipase loading could be decreased
to only 0.2 w/w, producing the same level of reaction enan-
tioselectivity. Therefore, Lipozyme TL-IM (0.2 w/w), vinyl
acetate (2.0 equiv.), in cycloh exane at rt for 48 h were de-
fined as the optimized reaction conditions for further
study.
Substrate Scope of -Allenols
The scope of the EKR reaction was then investigated by
using the optimal reaction conditions in Table 1 (Scheme 3).
We first studied the reactivity of -allenols with substitu-
ent at the para position on the benzene ring, such as chloro,
bromo, or trifluoromethyl group, and they are all success-
fully converted into the corresponding optically pure esters
kinetically, providing >1000 of S-factor in all cases. Reaction
enantioselectivity was decreased for -allenol 1d, bearing
one chloro group at the meta position. It is noteworthy to
mention that the esterification step became much slower
with a substituent at the ortho position due to the steric ef-
fect, and in this case Na
2CO3 was added to dramatically ac-
celerate the kinetic esterification. The benzyl group can also
be tolerated, as shown by the reaction outcomes of 1f. Since
low enantioselectivity was observed for electron-rich sub-
strates catalyzed by  lipase AK in the previous report,
12 we
subsequently focused on -allenols bearing electron-donat-
ing groups (EDG). The 4-me thoxy group on the benzene
ring led to a decreased S-factor in the EKR process, but still
almost three times higher than that catalyzed by lipase AK.
EKR performances by lipozyme TL-IM are significantly im-
proved for -allenol substrates bearing one or two 3-me-
thoxyl group(s). Bulky groups are greatly challenging to fit
the large pocket of lipase, th us generally resulting in low
enantioselectivity for such ki nds of substrates. However, to
our delight, EKR of -allenol 1j, bearing 2-naphthyl group,
gave equally excellent selectivity. An electron-donating
bulky group leads to a decreased S-factor of 127 in the reso-
lution of 1k. Finally, by increasing the catalyst loading to 2.0
w/w, reaction of -allenol 1l with a bulky group of 1-naph-
thyl can finish in 48 h, affording chiral ester ( R)-3l in 48%
yield with 98% ee, and the recovered (S)-1l in 47% yield with
96% ee.
We next studied the reactivity and selectivity of -alle-
nol rac-1m, bearing a completely aliphatic side chain. As
shown in Scheme 4, the kinetic resolution of rac-1m (1.0
mmol) under Lipozyme TL-IM produced the corresponding

ester (S)-3m in 35% yield with 88% ee, and ( R)-1m was re-
covered in 61% yield with 48% ee. Therefore, the S-factor
was observed to be 25 in this reaction.
With obtained optically pure -allenols, we then tested
synthetic applications of (S)-1a (Scheme 5). Silver-mediated
cyclization of ( S)-1a (>99% ee) delivered 2,5-dihydrofuran
(S)-4a in 85% yield with 98% ee,10a while cycloisomerization
of (S)-1a catalyzed by Shvo’s catalyst afforded 2,3-dihydro-
furan (S)-4b in 66% yield with >99% ee.11 These chiral oxy-
cycles are valuable building blocks in synthetic chemistry.
In conclusion, we have de veloped an efficient EKR
method of -allenols, realized by a commercially available
immobilized lipase, Lipozyme TL-IM. The S-factor of this ki-
netic resolution method was investigated to reach up to
>1000. The substrate scope has shown that not only elec-
tron-withdrawing groups, but also electron-donating
groups could be nicely tolerated on the benzene ring. -Al-
lenols bearing a bulky group were also compatible to deliv-
er chiral esters kinetically. This method offers an alternative
approach to access chiral -allenols and their esters with
high enantioselectivity, which will be of high value for the
synthesis of chiral oxycycles.
